readout.headline: Ship the test variant of the invoice template gallery, since it clearly beat control on invoices sent.
readout.summary: We tested the invoice template gallery by splitting users 50/50 between control and test, and tracked invoices sent as the primary metric and refund requests as the guardrail. The test variant converted 13% of users to sending an invoice, compared with 10% for control, a lift of 30.2%. The test has a 100% chance of being best, and refund requests did not get worse, so the code's rule for shipping was met. The experiment ran for 28 days with no sign of users seeing both variants or of a split mismatch.
details: Invoice sent: test 13% (390 of 3000 users) vs control 10% (300 of 3000 users)
Lift vs control: 30.2%, with a 95% interval of 12.3% to 49.7%
Chance of being best: test 100%, control 0%
Refunds requested: test 1.03% vs control 1.00%, with a 55.5% chance that test is worse
Runtime: 28 days; share of users who saw more than one variant: 0.0%
readout.next_step: The test template gallery will be rolled out to all users in place of control.

clarity.reason: The decision and invoice results are clear, but saying refunds did not get worse conflicts with the higher reported refund rate, and terms like 'chance of being best' add jargon.

runs.name: Annual billing toggle on pricing page

readout.headline: Results are invalid, so no decision can be made: the groups were not split as planned.
readout.summary: We tested an annual billing toggle on the pricing page, splitting users 50/50 between the current page and a version with the toggle. The groups did not come out the same size as planned, a sample ratio mismatch with a p-value below 0.001, which usually signals a bug in assignment or tracking. Because of this, the upgrade numbers cannot be trusted even though the test version appears to perform better. No user saw more than one variant, so cross-contamination is not the cause. The decision is therefore invalid and no variant can be declared a winner.
details: Runtime: 28 days, experiment stopped, minimum runtime of 14 days met
Control: 3000 users, 300 upgrades, 10% upgrade rate
Test: 2400 users, 312 upgrades, 13% upgrade rate
Sample ratio mismatch p-value: below 0.001 (limit 0.001)
Users who saw both variants: 0.0% (limit 5%)
Refund requests: 0.67% in both groups, no meaningful difference
readout.next_step: The team should investigate the assignment and tracking bug behind the sample ratio mismatch and rerun the experiment before drawing conclusions.

clarity.reason: The first line makes the decision clear, the uneven split and its implications are explained plainly, and the key numbers and next steps support the decision.

runs.name: One-click upgrade from the invoice list

readout.headline: Keep the current invoice flow: the one-click upgrade wins on upgrades but raises refund requests too much.
readout.summary: The one-click upgrade from the invoice list was tested against the current flow over 28 days, with 3000 users in each group. The test raised Upgrade completed from 10% to 13%, a clear win. However, Refunds requested rose from 1% to 2.5%, and that guardrail must not get worse. Because the test broke a guardrail, the code keeps the control and does not ship the test.

Refunds requested: control 1% vs test 2.5% (lift 153.5%), a clear regression
Support tickets opened: 2% vs 2.07%, no meaningful change (p-value 0.855)
Runtime 28 days; 0% of users saw more than one variant; sample ratio check p-value 1.000
readout.next_step: The control stays live and the team should investigate why the one-click upgrade increases refund requests before any retest.

clarity.reason: The decision and refund concern are clear upfront, with the key numbers included, though terms like “guardrail” and extra statistical details add some jargon.

runs.name: Default due date of 15 days instead of 30

readout.headline: Keep the current 30-day default due date; the 15-day test is likely better but its lift is below the 10% minimum worth shipping.
readout.summary: We tested a default due date of 15 days against the current 30 days over a 32-day run, with 30,000 users in each group. The 15-day test had a higher invoice-sent rate than control, and the chance it is better is high. However, the estimated lift of 5% falls below the 10% minimum lift our rules require before shipping. Support tickets were essentially unchanged between the two groups, so there is no guardrail concern. Because the lift does not clear the shipping bar, we keep the control.
